headline: US midterms deal Trump a major setback, Stephen Miller takes over as White House chief of staff, while your portfolio rides a broad green day led by MSFT and VGE.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft surged last night — up 2.38% to $543.23 USD. No single news catalyst, but the broader tech rally (NASDAQ up 2.54%) lifted it strongly, and Microsoft continues to benefit from investor enthusiasm around its AI products and cloud business. It's now sitting 22.6% above your cost base.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE had a solid session today, up 1.76% to $89.96. Emerging markets got a lift as the Aussie dollar slipped slightly (making overseas assets worth more in AUD terms) and global risk appetite improved on the back of Wall Street's strong night last night.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google climbed 1.7% last night to $288.75 USD, riding the broad NASDAQ rally. There was some mixed news — Alphabet reportedly sold $548M in a tech stock holding while keeping its SpaceX stake, and JPMorgan removed it from their analyst focus list. Neither is a major concern for long-term holders — the core business is intact.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS had a good day today, up 2.12% to $2.89. However, it's still down 57% from your cost base — a reflection of the prolonged lithium price slump. Scotiabank cut its price target on US lithium giant Albemarle citing a weaker lithium outlook, which is a headwind for the whole sector including Pilbara.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI bounced 1.13% today to $15.25, recovering some ground after what appears to have been a broader AI sector sell-off earlier in the week. Still sitting 19.26% below your purchase price — the AI theme is real but this ETF has been volatile. Long-term thesis is intact.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS climbed 1.03% today to $528.22, reflecting last night's strong US session (S&P 500 up 2.27%). This ETF tracks the whole US sharemarket, so a big night on Wall Street flows straight through to today's ASX price. Now sitting 2.43% above your cost base.

movers.name: DHHF (Diversified High Growth ETF)
movers.note: DHHF ticked up 0.73% today — a steady, unremarkable session. It holds a broad mix of global shares so it tends to move with the overall market. No specific news catalyst; just along for the ride on a broadly positive day.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG nudged up 0.16% today — essentially flat. It includes a large allocation to bonds and international shares, which muted some of today's equity gains. Nothing to worry about; it's doing what a diversified fund does.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two dipped 1.21% last night to $212.27 USD, the only red in your portfolio. No major bad news — analysts are actually bullish with a 37% upside price target, pointing to Take-Two's $8 billion bookings target for GTA VI. The dip looks like normal market noise ahead of a big product launch.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Lithium outlook stays tough
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals bounced 2.12% today but is still down 57% from your cost base. Scotiabank just cut its price target on US lithium peer Albemarle, flagging a lower lithium price outlook. The long-term electric vehicle story is still real, but there's no near-term catalyst. If you believe in lithium's 5-10 year future, sit tight — but be aware this one could stay subdued for a while yet.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI ETF recovering but still underwater
watch_today.detail: GXAI is up 1.13% today but still 19.26% below your purchase price. The AI sell-off earlier this week spooked markets but today's bounce suggests it was overdone. The long-term AI investment theme is very much intact — the RBA itself is talking about AI's economic impact. No reason to sell; consider whether today's dip-and-recover is a chance to top up if you believe in the thesis.

watch_today.title: TTWO: GTA VI hype building, ignore last night's dip
watch_today.detail: Take-Two fell 1.21% last night but analyst consensus remains strongly bullish — a 37% upside target, anchored to the company's $8 billion bookings target for GTA VI. There's even GTA VI merchandise appearing at Selfridges in London. This is a long-term bet on one of the biggest game launches in history. Last night's dip is noise.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Strong night, long-term AI story intact
watch_today.detail: Microsoft jumped 2.38% last night, now sitting 22.6% above your cost base. The AI and cloud narrative continues to drive it. No specific news catalyst tonight — just broad market strength. Nothing to do here except enjoy it.

watch_today.title: RBA rate outlook: Higher for longer warning
watch_today.detail: The Reserve Bank has flagged that Australia's AI data centre construction boom is adding to inflation pressures, which could keep interest rates higher for longer. This matters for your portfolio because higher rates tend to weigh on growth stocks and ETFs with tech exposure (like GXAI and VTS). Worth keeping an eye on the next RBA meeting for any shift in tone.

watch_today.title: Oil drops 3.6% — Middle East tension but supply fears ease
watch_today.detail: Crude oil fell sharply last night — down 3.59% to $87.57 USD. A Saudi oil pipeline was attacked overnight, causing a fire, but broader commentary suggests markets expect a post-conflict oil supply glut as Middle East tensions gradually ease. Lower oil is generally good for inflation and consumer spending, which is a mild positive for the broader sharemarket.

world.summary: The big stories today: US midterm elections hand Trump's Republicans a stinging defeat, Stephen Miller steps in as White House chief of staff, the Middle East remains on edge with a Saudi pipeline attack, and US-Iran nuclear talks quietly restart.

stories.title: Republicans routed in US midterm elections — Trump claims America took a 'giant step back'
stories.why_it_matters: The 2026 US midterm elections have delivered a significant blow to Donald Trump and the Republicans, with the party losing seats and control in key areas. Trump responded by claiming the US had taken a 'giant step back in history' and signalled he intends to lurch further right. For markets, this could mean more political gridlock in Washington — which historically isn't the worst thing for stocks, but it does cloud the outlook for big fiscal policies like tax cuts or tariffs that investors had been pricing in.

stories.title: Stephen Miller takes over as White House chief of staff
stories.why_it_matters: Hardline Trump adviser Stephen Miller — the architect of some of the administration's most controversial immigration and border policies — has been appointed White House chief of staff. This follows the midterm losses and signals Trump is doubling down on a more extreme policy agenda rather than moderating. Miller is widely seen as one of the most ideologically driven figures in Trump's orbit, and his elevation is likely to sharpen the administration's hard-line stance on immigration, trade and foreign policy.

stories.title: Saudi oil pipeline attacked, fire breaks out — Middle East on edge
stories.why_it_matters: An attack on a Saudi oil pipeline caused a fire overnight, adding another layer of tension to an already unstable Middle East. This comes as Iran conflict fears continue to simmer, and the Strait of Hormuz — through which about 20% of global oil flows — remains a pressure point. Despite the attack, oil prices actually fell sharply (down 3.6%), suggesting markets believe any supply disruption will be temporary and that a post-conflict glut is more likely. For you as an investor, sustained high oil prices would add to inflation, which keeps interest rates elevated.

stories.title: US and Iran quietly negotiating amid ongoing Middle East conflict
stories.why_it_matters: Despite the ongoing conflict and fiery rhetoric, the US and Iran are quietly holding back-channel negotiations, according to CNN. The talks are focused on nuclear limits and sanctions relief — essentially the same ground as previous deals. If successful, a deal could bring Iranian oil back to global markets, further pushing down oil prices and easing Middle East tensions. If they collapse, the risk of a broader regional conflict — involving Israel, Iran and proxy groups — rises significantly. This is one of the most important slow-burn geopolitical stories of 2026.

stories.title: Middle East conflict could push China needle coke prices to 3-year high
stories.why_it_matters: The Middle East conflict is disrupting the supply of needle coke — a key raw material used to make graphite electrodes for electric arc furnaces and, importantly, lithium-ion battery anodes. Benchmark Mineral Intelligence reports prices could hit a 3-year high. This matters for the battery and EV supply chain broadly, and could eventually feed into input costs for lithium producers like Pilbara Minerals. It's a secondary effect but one worth watching for PLS holders.

markets.summary: Wall Street had a cracking session last night — the S&P 500 jumped 2.27% and the NASDAQ surged 2.54%, likely driven by post-midterm relief as political uncertainty eased. The ASX followed with a quieter but positive session today, up just 0.1%. Oil dropped sharply, gold ticked higher, and the Aussie dollar was essentially flat.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Big night on Wall Street last night — up 2.27%. Markets likely reacting positively to the US midterm results, with political gridlock historically seen as a stable environment for stocks.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech led last night's rally with the NASDAQ up 2.54%. Strong gains across major tech names including MSFT and GOOG.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: The ASX had a subdued but positive close today, up just 0.1%. Markets here were already pricing in some of the overnight US gains from the previous session.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil fell hard last night — down 3.59% despite a Saudi pipeline attack. Markets appear to believe the conflict will ease and that a supply glut is coming. Lower oil helps inflation.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold nudged up 0.93% — investors still holding some safe-haven insurance amid Middle East tensions and US political uncertainty.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar slipped slightly — down 0.24% to 69.15 US cents. The RBA's warning about higher-for-longer rates is mixed for the AUD; watch for further moves this week.

politics.summary: A busy week in Australian politics: the RBA is warning that AI-driven inflation could keep rates higher for longer, Labor is facing internal chaos over Treasurer Jim Chalmers, the gas reservation debate is heating up in WA, and artists are taking on the PM over AI copyright laws.

stories.title: RBA warns AI data centre boom could keep Australian interest rates higher for longer
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia has flagged that the AI data centre construction boom is adding to inflation — pouring money into energy, land and construction in a way that's pushing prices up. Separately, the RBA notes that AI is slowly boosting productivity but the inflationary effects are coming first. The practical upshot: rates could stay higher for longer than many Australians were hoping. If you have a mortgage or are thinking about property, this matters. It also affects growth stocks and ETFs in your portfolio.

stories.title: Labor's internal war: Minister urges colleagues to stop undermining Treasurer Jim Chalmers
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government is showing cracks, with an unnamed minister publicly urging Labor colleagues to stop backgrounding against Treasurer Jim Chalmers. Reports of internal leaks undermining Chalmers have been circulating for weeks. This is significant because Labor's tax and economic agenda — including any changes to CGT (capital gains tax — the tax you pay when you sell an asset for a profit) or negative gearing — flows through the Treasurer's office. A weakened Chalmers means less political capital for big economic reforms.

stories.title: WA Premier Roger Cook demands hands off gas and GST ahead of Senate vote
stories.why_it_matters: Western Australia's Premier Roger Cook is demanding the federal government keep its hands off both gas reservation policy and the state's share of GST revenue, ahead of a crucial Senate vote. WA gets a larger slice of GST than other states and any reform is fiercely resisted. The gas reservation debate — whether gas producers should be forced to supply Australian consumers before exporting — is gaining momentum as east coast gas prices stay high. Labor is reportedly considering concessions to try to get a bill through.

stories.title: Australian artists urge PM Albanese to stop AI companies using their work without permission
stories.why_it_matters: A coalition of Australian artists — including some of PM Albanese's favourite musicians — have written an open letter urging the government to stop AI companies from scraping their work to train AI models without consent or payment. They want copyright law updated to require licences and compensation. The government is under pressure from both sides: the creative industry wants protection, while tech companies argue strict rules will hamper Australia's AI development. This feeds into the broader global copyright debate that could affect companies like Google and Microsoft, which run major AI platforms.

ai.summary: AI regulation is dominating today's AI news cycle globally and locally — from Europe pushing for a global incident-reporting system, to the RBA flagging AI's inflationary side effects in Australia. There's also a new open-source AI model launch from NEAR Protocol.

stories.title: Europe pushes for global AI incident reporting system
stories.why_it_matters: European think tank Bruegel is calling on Europe to lead the creation of a global compact — essentially an international agreement — where countries and companies must report AI incidents (like when an AI system causes harm or behaves dangerously). The idea is similar to how aviation safety works: mandatory incident reporting so everyone can learn from failures before they become disasters. This would have real implications for companies like Google and Microsoft, which would likely be required to report AI failures to regulators across multiple jurisdictions.

stories.title: RBA: AI is inflating costs now, productivity gains come later
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia has released analysis showing that AI is currently a net contributor to inflation — the data centre building boom, the energy required to run AI, and the investment pouring into the sector are all adding to cost pressures right now. The productivity benefits — where AI makes workers more efficient and lowers the cost of goods and services — are expected to come later, possibly years away. For everyday Australians, this means AI could be contributing to the high cost of living in the near term, even as it promises to reduce it over the long run.

stories.title: NEAR Protocol launches new open-source AI model — Qwen 3.8 27B
stories.why_it_matters: NEAR Protocol — a blockchain network — has launched a new AI model called Qwen 3.8 27B Abliterated for its AI Cloud service. What this means in plain terms: it's a large open-source language model (think a ChatGPT-style AI, but free to use and modify) that developers can run via NEAR's cloud platform. The 'abliterated' part refers to removing certain safety restrictions, making it more flexible for developers. It's part of a growing trend of open-source AI models competing with the closed models from Google and OpenAI.

stories.title: Australia's digital classrooms get a 'detox' — phones and devices restricted
stories.why_it_matters: Australian schools are rolling out 'digital detox' policies — restricting student use of phones and tablets in class as research mounts that constant digital distraction is hurting learning outcomes. While this isn't directly an AI story, it's part of the broader societal reckoning with technology in everyday life. It also has implications for how AI tools in education will be regulated and rolled out, as governments try to balance digital literacy with the proven harms of excessive screen time for children.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final wrapped up with the Roosters defeating the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. Post-match the drama continued, with ref controversy, a Broncos star's drink-driving ban handed down, and an Eels recruit facing suspension over a World Cup gesture.

stories.title: Roosters defeat Knights 19-18 in NRL Grand Final thriller
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters won the 2026 NRL Grand Final, defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in a one-point nail-biter at Accor Stadium on Sunday night. It was a dramatic finish, with post-match controversy erupting — Roosters captain Jarome Luai called out the referee, and reportedly 'stormed off' after the match, while Knights coach called the result 'diabolical'. A classic Grand Final that will be talked about for years.

stories.title: Broncos star handed drink-driving ban by NRL
stories.why_it_matters: An unnamed Brisbane Broncos player has been handed a ban by the NRL following a drink-driving charge. The NRL's integrity unit handed down the suspension today. It's another off-field headache for the Broncos, who've had a difficult year managing player behaviour issues both on and off the field.

stories.title: Eels recruit facing ban after referee gesture at Rugby League World Cup
stories.why_it_matters: A star new recruit for the Parramatta Eels is facing an NRL-imposed ban after making an offensive gesture towards a referee during the Rugby League World Cup. The incident is being reviewed by the NRL's match review committee and could result in a suspension that affects his availability at the start of next season. The Eels will be hoping to get the matter resolved quickly ahead of pre-season.

stories.title: Origin forward snubs Raiders, makes 'huge contract call' after PNG tour
stories.why_it_matters: A State of Origin forward has reportedly knocked back a deal with the Canberra Raiders, saying he has 'nothing against Canberra' but has made a different contract decision following the NRL's tour of Papua New Guinea. The tour to PNG has become an increasingly influential factor in player contract decisions, with several players expressing a desire to stay at clubs closer to the PNG fan base. The player's destination is yet to be confirmed.
